lessons.text:
The good leave,
the petty move in.
lessons.why: Why things are stuck: the great departs, the small arrives, and the people who care are the ones pushed out.
lessons.feedback: The Judgment says 'Of inferior people... The great departs, the small arrives', and the synthesis says the configuration 'blocks the people who care'. Reading great and small as good and petty people is fair. It explains why things are stuck without repeating 'hold back' or 'turn down', and it suits the Judgment page. Line lengths are 15 and 18. Glad to post it.

lessons.text:
Big cart, loaded,
somewhere to go.
lessons.why: Having a lot is only useful when it has a load to carry and a place to take it.
lessons.feedback: True to line 2 ('A great cart for loading. Having somewhere to go.') and concrete. It fits the lit line and adds something the copy doesn't have: plenty is only useful with a load and a road. The slang reading of 'loaded' is a small bonus. Fine to post.

lessons.text:
Follow, and find
what you look for.
lessons.why: Line 3 says plainly that following, one finds what one seeks.
lessons.feedback: The wording is in line 3 ('Following, one finds what one seeks'), but it is the flattest part of that line. It is abstract and sounds like a slogan. It has no link to the short's rest-at-nightfall theme and gives no picture. The concrete, surprising part of line 3 is the trade: 'Attached to the mature one. Losing the small child.' Try line 3 as 'Hold the grown one,\nlose the child.' (18/15), or line 2 reversed. Either says that following something means giving something else up, which the short does not say.

lessons.text:
Plan three days,
check three days.
lessons.why: The Judgment puts three days before a new start and three days after it, so a repair gets time on both sides.
lessons.feedback: The Judgment gives three days before the new start and three after, and the synthesis reads that as deliberating on both sides, so 'plan' and 'check' are fair. It is concrete and specific and fits the Judgment page. It turns the copy's 'rushed repairs don't hold' into a rule of thumb instead of repeating it. Good.

lessons.why: FIRE over THUNDER: the kings made penalties clear and established the law, so clarity comes first and the bite second.
lessons.feedback: True: 'The ancient kings made penalties clear and established the law.' 'Warn clearly' is a fair plain version of making penalties clear beforehand. It matches the picture well: FIRE/lightning for clarity over THUNDER for the bite. It is short and a little funny, and it adds a condition to 'bite down': say it plainly first. Glad to post.

lessons.text:
At the solstice,
kings stayed home.
lessons.why: Thunder inside the earth is energy returning underground; the Image says kings closed the passes and stayed put at the solstice to let it come back.
lessons.feedback: True to the Image: at the solstice the passes were closed, merchants did not travel, and the ruler did not tour. A concrete, slightly surprising historical fact backs up the short's 'Rest. Only rushing stops it' without repeating it. Its one weakness is that it doesn't point at the THUNDER-under-EARTH picture, but the picture carries that on its own. Good to post.

lessons.text:
Kings fed everyone
by the seasons.
lessons.why: The other half of the Image: the old kings fed all beings in step with the seasons, not forcing growth.
lessons.feedback: The Image does say this ('ancient kings nourished all beings in alignment with the seasons'), but viewers won't connect it to the thunder-under-heaven trigram picture, and 'kings fed everyone' teaches nothing about innocence or pretense. It is history trivia, not a takeaway. Line 5 is the surprising material and fits 'stop faking': 'An illness without pretense. Do not medicate. There will be happiness.' Try it as a line lesson: 'A real illness?\nDon't medicate.' Also possible is line 3's tethered ox (the traveler's gain is the townsperson's loss).

lessons.text:
Wine and rice
through a window.
lessons.why: Line 4: a jug of wine and a basket of rice handed through the window are enough, and in the end no fault.
lessons.feedback: True to line 4, and concrete and unusual, which is good. As written it is only an image with no point, close to the rejected 'Its shape: a watchtower.' A first-time viewer won't know what wine and rice through a window mean. The line's verdict is 'in the end, no fault': in a deep hole, a plain offering is enough. Add that point, e.g. 'Wine and rice\nare enough.' or 'A plain gift through\nthe window is enough' (shorten to fit 18). Keep line 4 as the source.

lessons.text:
A good time
to take a wife.
lessons.why: The Judgment's one concrete point: taking a wife resolves well.
lessons.feedback: The Judgment does say 'Taking a wife resolves well'. It is concrete, a little funny, and new to the short. But 'A good time to...' reads like a horoscope prediction, and it lets go of Influence's point about making room. It would reach 8 with a plainer quote that isn't a forecast, e.g. 'Taking a wife:\ngoes well.' Or use the body-part lines, which are the hexagram's most surprising material. Line 1: 'Influence in the big toes.' becomes 'It starts in\nthe big toes.' as a line lesson.

lessons.text:
Great power keeps
off wrong paths.
lessons.why: Thunder above heaven: the Image says the strong person does not tread where it is not right.
lessons.feedback: True to the Image, but it repeats the short: the meaning is 'Mostly, know what not to do' and the question is 'What won't you do with it?'. 'Keeps off wrong paths' is also stiff. Switch to line 3, which is vivid and funny: 'The ram butts the hedge and entangles its horns.' For example 'Ram butts hedge,\nhorns get stuck.' (16/16). The line also contrasts 'The petty person uses power. The realized person uses restraint', so the image carries the point on its own.

lessons.text:
Don't get ahead
like a squirrel.
lessons.why: Line 4 compares grabbing, darting progress to a squirrel that everyone can see for what it is.
lessons.feedback: True to 'Progressing like a squirrel. Sustained orientation: strained.' It is concrete and funny, 'get ahead' is a plain way to say 'progress', and it supports the short's 'character first, not strategy' without repeating it. Some translations say rat or hamster, but squirrel is what the input has. Good to post.

lessons.why: Water on the mountain cannot flow, and the Image says to turn inward and work on character.
lessons.feedback: 'Can't flow' comes from the synthesis and 'turns inward' from the Image, so it is true. But 'Turn inward' is vague and overlaps the short's 'The wall is the lesson'. The question-and-answer form also reads a bit cryptic. The line texts are better and repeat a pattern: 'Going forward: obstruction. Coming back: praise.' (line 1). A line lesson: 'Go on: blocked.\nCome back: praise.' (15/17). Or line 5 ('Great obstruction. Companions come.'), which pays off the short's 'ask for help': 'Badly stuck,\nfriends come.'

lessons.why: The Judgment asks how to make the offering and answers with two small baskets.
lessons.feedback: True to the Judgment's question and answer about the offering. Concrete, a bit surprising, and it fits the Judgment page. It lines up with the copy's 'give what you can' but gives it an object, so it reads as a payoff, not a repeat. Good to post.

lessons.text:
Even bad events
can increase you.
lessons.why: Line 3: increased through unfortunate events, no fault.
lessons.feedback: True to line 3 ('Increased through unfortunate events. No fault.'). It is a real surprise and adds to a short about opportunity. 'Can increase you' is awkward English. A plainer version: 'Even bad events\ncan add to you.' or 'Bad things can\nincrease you too.' Fix the phrasing and it is an 8.

lessons.why: The Judgment says to use this time to see the great person, without worry.
lessons.feedback: True to the Judgment ('Use this time to see the great person'). 'Someone above you' is a fair plain rendering. It is practical, fits a short about slow growth, avoids the 'don't worry' already used in the meaning, and suits the Judgment page. It is less surprising than the best lessons, but I would post it.

lessons.text:
For a revolution,
a new calendar.
lessons.why: Fire in the lake is revolution, and the Image answers it by organizing the calendar and the seasons.
lessons.feedback: True to the Image (organize the calendar, clarify the seasons). Concrete, a little surprising, and it rings true to history (revolutions often do bring new calendars). It adds to the copy's 'finish first' instead of repeating it. The sentence doesn't name fire and lake, but the trigram picture carries them. Good.

lessons.text:
Walk past people,
not seeing them.
lessons.why: The Judgment: walking through the courtyard, not seeing the people, no fault. Stillness inside while moving.
lessons.feedback:
True to the Judgment, and surprising. But on its own a viewer can take it as snubbing people, the opposite of the calm the hexagram teaches, and nothing says the stillness is inside you. Two options. Frame it: 'Walk through a crowd,
still inside.' (needs trimming to 18: 'Still inside,
even in a crowd.'). Or use line 5, 'Stilling the jaws. Words have order.', which answers the overthinking hook: 'Still your jaw;
words come in order' (shorten). The Red Fuji painting is also available here and would land at a glance, if the series needs a painting.

lessons.why: Thunder and lightning together: force and clarity at once, the pair the Image uses to judge cases.
lessons.feedback: Built from the synthesis (force and clarity), but abstract and generic. It sits close to the short's question 'What will you decide now?'. The Image's actual instruction is deciding disputes, and neither trigram picture makes 'see clearly, act with force' land. Abundance has striking line texts. Line 2/4: 'So abundant are the screens that the Big Dipper is visible at midday.' Line 6: 'So abundant his dwelling... desolate, no one there.' Try line 6: 'A huge house,\nno one inside.' (12/14). It is a real turn after 'Be the sun at noon'. Or line 2: 'So many screens,\nstars at noon.'

history.text:
Small people in,
good people out.
history.why: Standstill is when the small take over and the good step away, which says who the Judgment means by great and small.
history.feedback: True: the Judgment opens 'Of inferior people' and says 'the great departs, the small arrives', so reading great and small as people is fair. It tells a new viewer what Standstill is about (the wrong people rise) and gives the reason behind the short's 'hold back'. But it states the situation without a picture or a turn, and 'good people' is a gloss of 'the great'. For an 8, use a more specific line: line 3 is two characters, 'Embracing shame' (e.g. 'Wrong people in charge?\nYou hold the shame.' needs trimming to 18 chars), or line 5's 'What if it fails? tied to mulberry shoots'. Or keep this kind and word it closer to the text: 'The great leave,\nthe small arrive.'

history.text:
Harm often looks
like opportunity.
history.why: Line 1 warns that at the start of wealth, harmful ties come dressed as chances, so the first fix is keeping clear of them.
history.feedback: The point is in the synthesis ('the trouble looks like opportunity'), but the line itself only says 'No interaction with harm... difficulty, then no fault.' The sentence is a generic proverb with 'often' added. It could sit under any hexagram, has no picture in it, and says nothing about wealth. Tie it to the short's success hook and keep it plain: 'Doing well? Keep\nclear of harm.' Or use another line with a concrete image: line 2's big wagon for carrying it, or line 3's prince who offers his wealth to the Son of Heaven while a small man cannot.

history.text:
Keep the child,
lose the adult.
history.why: Line 2 shows that holding on to one thing costs you another, so following means choosing.
history.feedback: True to 'Attached to the small child. Losing the mature one.' It is concrete and a little startling. In the imperative, though, 'Keep the child, lose the adult' sounds like an instruction to keep the child, and a new viewer may take the child literally. The past-tense version ('Grabbed the kid,\nlost the adult.') reads as a report of a trade, which is what the line gives. Or make the choice plain: 'Cling to the small,\nlose the great.' It connects loosely to the short (holding on to work costs rest).

history.text:
Think three days
before and after.
history.why: The Judgment asks for three days before the new start and three after, the book's own timing for fixing decay.
history.feedback:
True: 'Three days before the new start, three days after.' The concrete number is the good part. 'Before and after' has no object on screen, so a viewer asks 'before and after what?' Also, 'think' before and after is close to the short's 'Rushed repairs don't hold'. Name the event: 'Three days before
the fix, three after' is too long. Try 'Before a big fix:
three days, then three.' (check the length) or 'Plan three days,
check three days.'

history.text:
Laws work when
all can see them.
history.why: Fire over thunder is clarity then force; the Image says the old kings made penalties clear, because a rule only works when people can see it.
history.feedback: The claim about visibility comes from the synthesis ('made them visible'). The Image itself only says the kings 'made penalties clear and established the law.' The sentence does not connect to the picture (FIRE over THUNDER), and it changes the subject from the short's personal 'bite down, deal with it' to public law, so it is abstract and does not end the short. Use the trigrams directly: 'Lightning shows,\nthunder hits.' Or pair the law with the order: 'Make it clear,\nthen enforce it.'

history.text:
At the solstice,
kings stayed home.
history.why: Thunder inside the earth is energy returning underground; the Image says kings closed the passes and stayed put at the solstice to let it come back.
history.feedback: True to the Image: at the solstice the passes were closed, merchants did not travel, and the ruler did not tour. A concrete, slightly surprising historical fact backs up the short's 'Rest. Only rushing stops it' without repeating it. Its one weakness is that it doesn't point at the THUNDER-under-EARTH picture, but the picture carries that on its own. Good to post.

history.text:
Don't force it.
Match the season.
history.why: Thunder under heaven is things being what they are; the Image says the old kings fed all beings by the seasons instead of forcing them.
history.feedback: The Image says the kings 'nourished all beings in alignment with the seasons'. 'Don't force it' comes from the synthesis. The result is stock self-help advice with nothing to do with Innocence or the short's 'be straight, stop faking', and it doesn't use the THUNDER under HEAVEN picture. This hexagram's lines are much stronger. Line 3: 'Innocent, yet\nthe ox is taken.' (a passer-by takes the tethered ox and the villager is blamed), which is surprising and concrete. Line 5: an illness you didn't cause needs no medicine, e.g. 'Didn't cause it?\nNo need for medicine.' (trim to 18). Switching to a line also avoids two 'lines' lessons in a row at 24-25.

history.text:
Stuck? Pass food
through a window.
history.why: Line 4 has plain food handed through a window in the pit, a small concrete step that is enough to get through.
history.feedback: True to the line (wine, rice and clay vessels handed through the window, no fault), and the image is concrete and a little funny. 'Stuck?' turns it into an odd hack. A viewer can't tell who passes food to whom or why that helps, and 'Stuck?' echoes the hook 'One problem after another?'. Keep the objects and the verdict, which is the surprise: 'Food through\na window: no fault.' Or 'Plain food through\na window is enough.' This also answers the short's question about a small next step.

history.text:
Taking a wife
goes well.
history.why: The Judgment says influence goes well when it ends in marriage: being open to someone leads to commitment.
history.feedback: The Judgment says this word for word, and it is plain and a little surprising. On screen alone, 'Taking a wife goes well' reads like an omen or a fortune cookie, and it is gendered with no framing. It also has little to do with the short's 'make room, the full can't take anything in'. Frame it as what influence is for: 'Real influence\nends in marriage.' Or use the body sequence in the lines, which fits the hook 'Listening, but already decided?': line 6 is influence in the jaws, cheeks and tongue, e.g. 'All talk: jaw,\ncheeks, tongue.'

history.text:
The best use of
power: restraint.
history.why: Thunder above heaven is the most force in the highest place, and the Image uses it mainly to stay off wrong paths.
history.feedback: True, but it repeats the short: the meaning is 'Mostly, know what not to do' and the question is 'What won't you do with it?'. 'The best use of power: restraint' is the same point again, more abstract, and the phrasing is a little mannered. Use a line with a picture: line 3, the ram butting the hedge until its horns get stuck ('Ram hits hedge.\nHorns get stuck.'), or line 5, losing the ram with ease.

history.text:
Don't get ahead
like a squirrel.
history.why: Line 4 compares grabbing, darting progress to a squirrel that everyone can see for what it is.
history.feedback: True to 'Progressing like a squirrel. Sustained orientation: strained.' It is concrete and funny, 'get ahead' is a plain way to say 'progress', and it supports the short's 'character first, not strategy' without repeating it. Some translations say rat or hamster, but squirrel is what the input has. Good to post.

history.text:
Blocked outside?
Work on yourself.
history.why: Water stuck on the mountain cannot flow, and the Image says to turn inward and build character.
history.feedback: The Image says 'turns inward to cultivate character', but the sentence restates the short. 'Blocked outside?' echoes the hook 'Hit a wall?', and 'work on yourself' is the meaning 'The wall is the lesson' said again. It is also generic self-help and ignores the WATER on MOUNTAIN picture. Either use the picture ('Water stuck\non a mountain.') or a line: line 1 says going on meets obstruction and coming back meets praise ('Going: blocked.\nComing back: praised.'). Avoid line 5 (friends come), which would repeat the short's 'ask for help'.

history.text:
A small offering
is enough.
history.why: The Judgment says two small baskets will do for the offering: when there is sincerity, size doesn't matter.
history.feedback: True, but it drops the only concrete thing in the Judgment, the two small baskets. 'A small offering is enough' is also close to the short's 'give what you can'. Put the object back: 'Two small baskets\nare enough.' That way the viewer sees the specific, humble detail on the Judgment page.

history.text:
Even bad events
can make you grow.
history.why: Line 3 says one is increased through unfortunate events, with no fault.
history.feedback: True to 'Increased through unfortunate events. No fault.' But 'Even bad events can make you grow' is the familiar 'what doesn't kill you' line, so a viewer learns nothing surprising, and it has no picture. Keep the book's word to make it strange: 'Increased by\nbad luck. No fault.' Or use line 6, which is concrete and funny and warns against the short's opposite: 'Help no one, and\nsomeone hits you.' (the line: increases no one, someone strikes him).

history.text:
Go see the person
who matters.
history.why: The Judgment says to use this time to see the great person: growth goes faster with the right person on your side.
history.feedback: The wording comes from the synthesis. The Judgment says 'see the great person'. 'The person who matters' is vague on screen and sounds like networking advice, and it doesn't use the Judgment page's other concrete detail (advance south, do not worry; the short already uses 'don't worry'). Say it plainly: 'Go see someone\nwho can help.' Or change kind to line 3, 'Pushing upward into an empty city': 'Rising into\nan empty city.', which is concrete and surprising (nothing stands in the way).

history.text:
Big change? First
set the calendar.
history.why: Fire inside the lake is change, and the Image answers it by setting the calendar and naming the seasons.
history.feedback: Mostly true: the Image says the realized person 'organizes the calendar and clarifies the seasons', but 'First' is not in the text. The answer is concrete and surprising (revolution answered with a calendar). However, 'Big change?' echoes the hook 'Making a big change...', and 'First' echoes the meaning 'finish first'. Drop both: 'Kings answered it\nwith a calendar.' Or 'Change? Name\nthe new season.'

history.text:
Still your jaw,
words make sense.
history.why: Hokusai's Red Fuji (c. 1830-1832) is one still mountain; line 5 says still the jaw and your words come out in order.
history.feedback: True to line 5 ('Stilling the jaws. Words have order.'), but it doesn't fit its picture: Red Fuji shows a mountain, and the sentence is about a jaw. The approved painting lesson works because the sentence describes what is on screen ('Friends at lunch, holding together'). 'Still your jaw' is also an odd phrase and the comma splice reads awkwardly. Either keep the painting and write about the mountain (the Image: two mountains, thoughts don't go beyond one's position), avoiding the short's 'stay with where you are now', or switch kind to line 5 with plainer words: 'Hold your tongue,\nwords come in order.' Note the short's hook is about overthinking, not talking.

history.text:
Fire to see,
thunder to act.
history.why: Fire and thunder together are clarity and force at once, which the Image uses to decide cases while the moment lasts.
history.feedback: It fits the FIRE and THUNDER labels exactly, is short and parallel, and gives the viewer a way to read the two trigrams, so it works with the short's 'What will you decide now?'. It is a gloss of the trigrams (from the synthesis) rather than what the Image instructs, which is to decide disputes and carry out punishments, so it is a little abstract. It also covers the same idea as 21 (the same trigrams swapped); check that the two don't read alike when watched back to back. For an 8, add the Image's action: 'Clear and strong:\ntime to judge.' Or keep it as is if 21 changes.

history.text:
The great leave,
the small arrive.
history.why: Standstill is when the wrong people rise and the right ones go, the reason behind holding back.
history.feedback: The Judgment does say 'The great departs, the small arrives.' Read cold, though, 'the great' and 'the small' could mean anything: sizes, things, people. The viewer gets no takeaway in two seconds. The synthesis makes it concrete: the people who care are blocked and the ones who don't are doing fine. Say it about people, e.g. 'Good people leave,\nsmall ones rise.' Or line 1, pulling up thatch grass, which comes up by the roots together with its kind, for something more concrete.

history.text:
Big cart, loaded,
somewhere to go.
history.why: Having a lot is only useful when it has a load to carry and a place to take it.
history.feedback: True to line 2 ('A great cart for loading. Having somewhere to go.') and concrete. It fits the lit line and adds something the copy doesn't have: plenty is only useful with a load and a road. The slang reading of 'loaded' is a small bonus. Fine to post.

history.text:
Grabbed the kid,
lost the adult.
history.why: Following one thing costs you another; line 2 reports the trade without judging it.
history.feedback: The line 2 synthesis says 'You grabbed the kid and lost the adult', and it is memorable and a little funny. Out of context, though, 'grabbed the kid' reads like a kidnapping, and nothing tells the viewer this is about choosing what to follow. Use the hexagram's own verb, e.g. 'Follow the kid,\nlose the adult.' That keeps the joke and makes the trade clear.

history.text:
Plan three days,
check three days.
history.why: The Judgment puts three days before a new start and three days after it, so a repair gets time on both sides.
history.feedback: The Judgment gives three days before the new start and three after, and the synthesis reads that as deliberating on both sides, so 'plan' and 'check' are fair. It is concrete and specific and fits the Judgment page. It turns the copy's 'rushed repairs don't hold' into a rule of thumb instead of repeating it. Good.

history.text:
State the penalty,
then enforce it.
history.why: Lightning then thunder: the old kings made penalties clear first, then set the law.
history.feedback: The Image says penalties were made clear and the law established. 'Enforce' goes a little past 'established the law'. The bigger problems: the sentence never touches the picture (FIRE over THUNDER), so the trigrams and the words don't connect, and 'enforce it' repeats the copy's 'bite down'. Line kind is ruled out here (20 and 22 are line lessons). Tie it to the flash and then the bang, e.g. 'Lightning shows,\nthunder hits.' Or 'See the rule,\nthen feel it.'

history.text:
Not upright?
Start nothing.
history.why: The Judgment says that without uprightness there is calamity and going forward is not supported. (Kept off kind line: 26 and 27 are accepted line lessons, so a line here would make three in a row.)
history.feedback: Accurate to the Judgment, but it repeats the short's meaning ('be straight / stop faking') in a sterner voice, and it is abstract. Line is ruled out (26 and 27 are line lessons). Better options: the lines kind, from the Image, 'Thunder under heaven: all things without pretense', e.g. 'Thunder, sky,\nnothing faked.' Or a judgment sentence that adds something new. If the kinds can be shuffled, line 3 (the tethered ox the traveller takes, 'Innocent, yet\nthe ox is taken') or line 5 (an illness without pretense, don't medicate) is far more surprising.

history.text:
Food through a
window: no fault.
history.why: In the pit, wine and rice handed through a window is enough; the book finds no fault in it.
history.feedback: True to line 4 and concrete. But the break 'Food through a / window' strands 'a', and 'no fault' is book jargon a new viewer won't read as 'this is enough'. Say what the synthesis says, that a small act of help is fine even in the pit, e.g. 'Help can come\nthrough a window.' Or 'Wine and rice,\nthrough a window.'

history.text:
Real influence
ends in marriage.
history.why: The Judgment gives taking a wife as where mutual influence goes: it becomes a commitment.
history.feedback: It overclaims. The Judgment says taking a wife resolves well; it does not say that real influence ends in marriage. That reading comes from the synthesis's commentary. As written, it also sounds prescriptive and dated, and it has nothing to do with the short's 'make room'. Line is ruled out (30 and 32 are line lessons). Use the lines kind with the Image, e.g. 'A lake sits\nup on a mountain.' Or keep judgment but say only what it says, e.g. 'A good time\nto marry.' If kinds can shift, the body-part lines (toes, calves, thighs, then jaws and tongue) are the funny, specific material.

history.text:
Thunder on high:
watch your step.
history.why: Thunder above heaven is great power, and the Image says the strong person does not tread where it is not proper. (The ram line was not possible: 33 and 35 are accepted line lessons, so a line here would make three in a row.)
history.feedback: The Image supports 'does not tread where improper', but 'watch your step' weakens it into a general be-careful idiom. It also repeats the copy almost exactly ('know what not to do' / 'What won't you do with it?'), so it adds nothing after the question. Line kind is blocked by the neighbours, so the ram is out. At least name the Image plainly, e.g. 'Thunder over sky:\nskip wrong roads.' Or reshuffle the neighbours so 34 can take line 3 or line 6 (the ram stuck in the hedge), which is the concrete, funny material here.

history.text:
Water stuck
on a mountain.
history.why: The two trigrams make the picture of obstruction: water that cannot flow off the mountain.
history.feedback: True to the Image ('water upon the mountain') and the synthesis ('can't flow, just sits'). It fits the trigram picture exactly and works like the approved 'Unseen water under the earth'. It only pictures the name, though, and gives no takeaway. That's acceptable next to the copy's 'ask for help', but a line such as line 1 ('Going forward: obstruction. Coming back: praise') would teach something new, e.g. 'Stuck ahead?\nCome back.'

history.text:
Two small baskets
are enough.
history.why: The Judgment asks how to make the offering and answers with two small baskets.
history.feedback: True to the Judgment's question and answer about the offering. Concrete, a bit surprising, and it fits the Judgment page. It lines up with the copy's 'give what you can' but gives it an object, so it reads as a payoff, not a repeat. Good to post.

history.text:
Bad luck adds
to him. No fault.
history.why: Line 3 says bad events can add to you when you walk the middle way.
history.feedback: The source is right: line 3 says 'Increased through unfortunate events. No fault.' The phrasing is the problem. 'Adds to him' has no referent and reads like a mistranslation, and 'No fault' is jargon. It is the most striking line in the hexagram, so say it plainly, e.g. 'Even bad events\ncan increase you.' Or 'Bad luck can\nadd to you too.'

history.text:
Go see someone
who can help.
history.why: The Judgment tells the one rising to go and see the great person. (Line 3 was not possible: 44 and 45 are accepted line lessons.)
history.feedback: True to the Judgment ('see the great person'), but 'who can help' flattens it into generic self-help. It also echoes 39's copy ('Who could you ask?'), so a viewer watching the series back to back sees it again. Line is blocked by 44 and 45. The lines kind with the Image is concrete and fits 'small steps, piled up' without repeating it, e.g. 'A tree grows\ninside the earth.'

history.text:
For a revolution,
a new calendar.
history.why: Fire in the lake is revolution, and the Image answers it by organizing the calendar and the seasons.
history.feedback: True to the Image (organize the calendar, clarify the seasons). Concrete, a little surprising, and it rings true to history (revolutions often do bring new calendars). It adds to the copy's 'finish first' instead of repeating it. The sentence doesn't name fire and lake, but the trigram picture carries them. Good.

history.text:
Cross the yard,
not seeing people.
history.why: The Judgment describes a stillness so deep you cross the courtyard and nothing there takes hold of you. (Line 5 was not possible: 53 and 54 are accepted line lessons.)
history.feedback: True to the Judgment, but 'not seeing people' reads as ignoring people or being absent-minded, not as stillness inside. A new viewer would get the wrong idea. Keep the walk and make the stillness explicit, e.g. 'Still inside,\nwhile you walk.' Or use the painting option this hexagram offers, Hokusai's Red Fuji: one still mountain lands at a glance, and the series is under its 10% painting target.

history.text:
Clear and strong:
time to judge.
history.why: With lightning and thunder together, the Image says to decide disputes and carry out penalties.
history.feedback: True to the Image (decide disputes, carry out punishments), but 'time to judge' is abstract and ambiguous (as in 'being judgmental'?). It also repeats the copy's question 'What will you decide now?', and its source is almost the same as 21's lightning-and-thunder penalties, so series viewers get it twice. Line is blocked by 53 and 54. If it stays lines, tie the two trigrams to seeing and acting, e.g. 'Lightning to see,\nthunder to act.' If the kinds can move, line 2 or line 4 ('So abundant are the screens that the Big Dipper is visible at midday') is the surprising material, e.g. 'Stars at noon:\ntoo many screens.'

history.text:
Good people leave,
petty ones arrive.
history.why: The Judgment says the great departs and the small arrives; the synthesis says the people who care are blocked while the ones who don't do fine.
history.feedback: True: the Judgment reads 'Of inferior people... The great departs, the small arrives', and the synthesis supports reading it as people. It is plain, it fits the Judgment page, and it gives a reason behind the short's 'hold back / don't take the bad deal'. It stops short of 8 because it is bleak and general, and 'good people' is more moralizing than 'the great'. For something a viewer would send on, use line 5 as a line lesson. The standstill ends and the great person's reaction is 'What if it fails? What if it fails?': "It ends. Still:\n'What if it fails?'" (14/18). Or keep the Judgment with "The great leave,\nthe small arrive."

history.text:
Follow the kid,
lose the adult.
history.why: Line 2: attached to the small child, losing the mature one; whatever you follow, you give something up.
history.feedback: True to line 2 ('Attached to the small child. Losing the mature one'). It is concrete and a little funny, and it adds to a short that is about stopping work at night. Without the trade-off idea, though, a new viewer reads it as a riddle, or as parenting advice. 'Follow the kid' also changes the text's 'attached to'. Make the trade explicit: "Hold the child,\nlose the grown-up." (14/16), or "Pick the kid, and\nyou lose the adult." (16/18). Line 3 is the mirror image and ends better ('Following, one finds what one seeks') if a positive ending suits the drop.

history.text:
Lightning: see it.
Thunder: feel it.
history.why: Fire over thunder: the kings made penalties clear first, then enforced them; you see the flash, then feel the bang.
history.feedback: The 'see it / feel it' comes from the synthesis, but it leaves out the point, which is that the kings made penalties clear first and then enforced them. On screen it becomes a fact about weather, so a viewer learns nothing about Biting Through. Best fix: line 4 as a line lesson, 'Biting through dried meat on the bone. Finding metal arrows.' It is concrete, surprising and matches 'bite down': "Tough meat, with\narrowheads inside." (15/18). If you keep the trigrams, say the point: "Make the rules\nclear, then enforce."

history.text:
Thunder under sky,
nothing pretends.
history.why: The Image: thunder moves beneath heaven and all things are without pretense.
history.feedback: True to the Image ('all things without pretense'), but it restates the short's copy ('be straight', 'stop faking', 'where are you performing?'), so it adds nothing. 'Nothing pretends' is also a little mannered. Use line 2, 'Not plowing for the harvest', which is concrete and new: "Plow without\neyeing the harvest." (11/18). Line 3, the tethered ox, also works if you want to show that innocence can still lose: "A passer-by takes\nthe tethered ox." (17/16).

history.text:
Help can come
through a window.
history.why: Line 4: wine and rice handed through a window; even in the pit, a small plain act of help is enough.
history.feedback: True to line 4 (wine, rice and clay vessels handed through the window; no fault). It adds a new idea, that small help counts, to 'keep moving'. As written, 'help through a window' sounds like a metaphor, and the objects that make the line memorable are gone. Put them back: "Wine and rice,\nthrough the window." (13/18), or "In the pit, rice\npassed through a window" if you can fit it. The concrete version is the one a viewer would send on.

history.text:
A lake sits
up on a mountain.
history.why: The Image: a lake atop the mountain, the low thing resting on the high one.
history.feedback: It restates the Image's picture ('A lake atop the mountain'), and the split-trigram visual already shows LAKE over MOUNTAIN. Like the rejected 'Its shape: a watchtower', it teaches nothing and leaves out what influence means. The meaning ('receive through emptiness') is already in the copy. Switch to a line lesson. The line texts track influence up the body from the big toes to the jaw and tongue, which is surprising and a little funny. Line 1: "Influence starts\nin the big toes." (16/15). Line 6 also works: "Last, it reaches\nthe jaw and tongue."

history.text:
Thunder over sky:
avoid wrong paths.
history.why: Thunder above heaven: with great power, the realized person does not tread where it is improper.
history.feedback: True to the Image, but it repeats the short's meaning ('Mostly, know what not to do') and question ('What won't you do with it?'). 'Avoid wrong paths' is also vague. Use line 3 as a line lesson: 'The ram butts the hedge and entangles its horns.' It is concrete, funny, and shows what happens to power without restraint: "Ram hits hedge,\nhorns get stuck." (14/15). Line 5, 'Loses the ram with ease', could follow as a softer alternative.

history.text:
Water can't flow:
work on yourself.
history.why: Water upon the mountain cannot flow; the realized person turns inward to cultivate character.
history.feedback: True to the Image; 'can't flow' comes from the synthesis. But 'work on yourself' is generic self-help, and it overlaps the copy's 'The wall is the lesson'. Line 2 would be a standout: 'obstruction upon obstruction. It is not a personal matter.' It is plain, a little funny, and people forward it: "Blocked again?\nIt's not personal." (13/17). The repeated pattern in lines 1, 3, 4 and 6 also works: "Push on: blocked.\nTurn back: praise." (16/17).

history.text:
Even bad events
can increase you.
history.why: Line 3: increased through unfortunate events, no fault; misfortune becomes material for growth.
history.feedback: True to line 3 ('Increased through unfortunate events. No fault'). It is plain, surprising, and new next to 'go now'. It falls short of 8 because it reads like a self-help poster; 'increase you' is a slightly odd phrase and nothing concrete is shown. You could try "Bad luck can\nadd to you too." Line 2, 'ten pairs of tortoise shells. One cannot refuse', is the concrete option: "Ten tortoise shells:\nyou can't refuse." (18/16), but it covers a different point.

history.text:
A tree grows
inside the earth.
history.why: The Image: within the earth, wood grows, pushing upward.
history.feedback: It restates the Image's picture and gives no meaning; the meaning ('accumulating small things') is already in the copy. It also clashes with the visual: the trigrams are labelled EARTH over WIND, and a viewer won't see how WIND becomes 'a tree'. Switch to a line lesson. Line 3, 'Pushing upward into an empty town', is surprising and new: "No one stops you:\nan empty town." (16/14). Line 2, where a modest offering is enough if you are sincere, is another option.

history.text:
Like the mountain:
still as you walk.
history.why: Hokusai's Red Fuji shows one still mountain; the Judgment has you walk through the courtyard with your back stilled, still inside while you move.
history.feedback: Supported by the Judgment ('walking through the courtyard... stilling the back') and its synthesis, and it adds 'still while moving' to 'pause'. But 'still as you walk' is a slightly mannered paradox, and the Red Fuji painting shows a mountain, not someone walking, so picture and sentence only half meet. For a short about overthinking, line 5 fits better: 'Stilling the jaws. Words have order.' "Still your jaw:\nyour words line up." (13/18). Keep the painting only if the series needs painting quota; a plainer Judgment wording would be "Walk the yard,\nstill inside."

history.text:
Bright and loud:
settle disputes.
history.why: Thunder and lightning arrive together, and the realized person decides disputes while there is both clarity and force.
history.feedback: True to the Image (thunder and lightning; decides disputes), but 'settle disputes' repeats the question 'What will you decide now?'. 'Bright and loud' also ties the thunder and lightning only loosely to the lesson. Lines 2 and 4 have the book's most striking image: at the height of abundance the screens are so thick that the Big Dipper shows at midday. As a line lesson: "So much shade, you\nsee stars at noon." (17/16). It is concrete and surprising, and it answers 'At your peak and worried?'. Note that 7 of these 12 lessons are the 'lines' kind (31, 34 and 39 among them). Moving several to line lessons, as suggested, would also fix the mix.

history.text:
The great leave,
the small arrive.
history.why: The Judgment gives the reason to hold back: in a standstill the great depart and the small arrive.
history.feedback: The Judgment does say 'The great departs, the small arrives.' The lesson copies that line without explaining it, though. A viewer reading 'the great' and 'the small' for two seconds can't tell whether they mean people, things or luck, so it lands as a riddle. It fits the Judgment page and doesn't repeat the copy. Plainer wording, still from the Judgment and its synthesis: 'The good go,\nthe petty come.' or 'The ones who care\nget no backing.'

history.text:
Hold the child,
lose the grown-up.
history.why: Line 2 says following one thing means losing another: attached to the small child, you lose the mature one.
history.feedback: Line 2 does say 'Attached to the small child. Losing the mature one.' The picture is concrete, has some bite and suits the lit line. It also brings a new idea after the rest-at-nightfall copy. The problem is that it reads like parenting advice: the point, that following one thing costs you another, doesn't come through. Keep the image and add the trade, for example 'Follow the small,\nlose the big.' Or keep the current text if the author wants it concrete; it's close to 8.

history.text:
Make the penalty
clear, then act.
history.why: Lightning then thunder: the ancient kings made penalties clear before enforcing the law, so the bite comes after the warning.
history.feedback: The Image says the kings 'made penalties clear and established the law'. 'Then act' is a light gloss on 'established the law', and it maps well onto FIRE (clarity) over THUNDER (action). It adds something to the bite-down copy. The weak spot is 'penalty', which sounds legal and cold, so it isn't something anyone would send to a friend. Something warmer from the same Image: 'Warn clearly,\nthen bite.' This short also has a strong painting (Hodler's Woodcutter), but the painting duplicates the copy's 'bite down' message, so lines is the better kind.

history.text:
Feed each thing
in its season.
history.why: The Image has the ancient kings nourish all beings in step with the seasons, rather than forcing growth.
history.feedback: The Image does say the kings nourished all beings in step with the seasons. That half of the Image has little to do with Innocence or with the HEAVEN over THUNDER picture, though, and the sentence reads as generic gardening advice. Nobody learns what 'without pretense' means from it. The lines have more surprising material. Line 3: 'A tethered ox — the traveler's gain is the townsperson's loss' (innocent, and you still lose), e.g. 'Innocent, and\nstill you lose.' Line 2: not plowing for the harvest. Line 5 (illness without pretense, don't medicate) is vivid, but it reads as health advice, so avoid it.

history.text:
Wine and rice,
through a window.
history.why: In the pit, line 4 has wine, rice and clay vessels handed through a window, and no fault: small help counts.
history.feedback: True to line 4, and the most concrete of this batch: wine, rice and a window make a real picture. The takeaway sits only in the 'why' (small help counts, no fault) and never appears on screen. A viewer gets the objects without the point, which risks the problem the author had with 'a watchtower'. Put the point in: 'Small help, passed\nthrough a window.' (16/15 characters). That would likely be an 8.

history.text:
Not a crush:
a marriage.
history.why: The Judgment says taking a wife resolves well: the book's influence is the kind that ends in commitment.
history.feedback: The Judgment says 'Taking a wife resolves well', and the synthesis says 'Not flirtation... Marriage.' The lesson is punchy and a little funny, and it adds something new to the make-room copy. But the 'X: Y' shape with no subject is close to the rejected 'Its shape: a watchtower', and nothing tells the viewer that the influence is what leads to marriage. Say it outright: 'Real pull ends\nin a marriage.' or 'This kind of pull\nends in marriage.'

history.text:
The risk isn't
abuse. It's drift.
history.why: The Judgment asks only for sustained orientation, because the danger of great power is forgetting to check your direction.
history.feedback: The actual Judgment is only 'Sustained orientation is supported.' The point comes from the app's synthesis, and the Judgment page shown won't back it up. It repeats the copy's 'check your aim', and the 'isn't X, it's Y' shape is mannered. The sentence also breaks awkwardly across the two screen lines. Use line 3 or line 6 instead: the ram butts the hedge and its horns get stuck. It's concrete and funny, and it's the book's own warning about power. For example, line 6: 'A ram butts the\nhedge, gets stuck.' (15/18 characters).

history.text:
One way is shut,
another is open.
history.why: The Judgment says the northeast is not supported but the southwest is: a block in one direction is not a block everywhere.
history.feedback: True to the Judgment (southwest supported, northeast not), and plain. It sounds like the 'one door closes, another opens' cliché, so it teaches nothing specific to the I-Ching. The rest of the Judgment, seeing the great person, overlaps with the copy's 'ask for help'. The lines repeat a pattern that's more distinctive: going forward, obstruction; coming back, praise, connection or ripeness. Line 1: 'Go on: blocked.\nTurn back: praised.' That teaches the hexagram's actual idea, that you retreat and regroup.

history.text:
You can gain
from bad events.
history.why: Line 3 says one is increased through unfortunate events, with no fault.
history.feedback: Line 3 does say 'Increased through unfortunate events. No fault.' The lesson is plain and adds a twist to the go-now copy. As written, though, it reads like a self-help poster, and 'bad events' is flat. The line's specifics (sincerity, the middle way, the seal of office) are lost. Tighter: 'Even bad luck\ncan add to you.' It stays a 6 or 7 either way. The paradox is the interesting part, so let the wording show it.

history.text:
Go see the one
who matters.
history.why: The Judgment says to use this time to see the great person: rising includes going to the people who can help.
history.feedback: True to the Judgment ('Use this time to see the great person'). On its own, 'the one who matters' reads as romantic, so the meaning is unclear at a glance. It also sits next to the copy's 'don't worry', which comes from the same Judgment. Plainer: 'Go see someone\nwho can help.' Better, use line 3, 'Pushing upward into an empty town': 'Climbing up into\nan empty town.' (16/13 characters). It's concrete and surprising, meaning rising meets no resistance, and it fits the lit-line picture. That also helps with too many judgments (see below).

history.text:
Walk the yard,
still inside.
history.why: The Judgment has someone walk through the courtyard without seeing the people: stillness is inside, not a frozen body.
history.feedback: The Judgment does have someone walking through the courtyard without seeing the people. 'Still inside' is the synthesis's reading, not the text. 'Walk the yard' sounds like prison slang, and the sentence as a whole is cryptic. Use line 5: 'Stilling the jaws. Words have order.' That gives 'Still your jaw,\nand words line up.' (14/17 characters). It's concrete and a little funny, and it answers the overthinking hook directly. Or use the Hokusai Red Fuji painting if the painting quota allows.

history.text:
Don't spend noon
on the afternoon.
history.why: The sun at midday will set; the Judgment says not to worry, so do not waste the peak worrying about the decline.
history.feedback: The source is the synthesis, not the Judgment. It's clever wordplay, but mannered, and it repeats the copy, which already says 'don't worry' and 'Be the sun at noon'. The lesson adds almost nothing. The lines are surprising and specific. Line 6: a huge house, screened off, and at the gate no one there for three years ('A huge house,\nand no one there.' 12/17). Or lines 2/3: so much shade that stars show at midday. Either gives the downside of abundance without spelling out the copy's own point. Series note: 7 of these 12 are judgment, well over the ~25% target. Move 34, 46 and 52 to line lessons to rebalance, and check that no three neighbours share a kind.

history.text:
The good go,
the petty come.
history.why: The Judgment names the standstill: inferior people, the great departs and the small arrives, so the good people leave and the petty ones take their place.
history.feedback:
True: 'The great departs, the small arrives' plus 'Of inferior people'. The synthesis supports reading it as the people who care being pushed out. It is plain, fits the Judgment page, and says something new after 'hold back / don't take the bad deal': why things are stuck. It is a little abstract and reads like a proverb. For a more concrete end, line 5 is funny and specific: 'What if it fails? What if it fails?' tied to mulberry shoots. That would give 'Worried it'll fail?
Tie it down.' (line kind, if neighbours allow). If it stays a judgment, 'The good leave,
the petty move in.' is slightly more conversational.

history.text:
Follow the small,
lose the big.
history.why: Line 2: attached to the small child, losing the mature one; whatever you follow costs you something else.
history.feedback:
True to line 2: 'Attached to the small child. Losing the mature one.' Turning 'small child / mature one' into 'the small / the big' loses the concrete picture, which was the interesting part. What is left is an abstract trade-off. It also has no link to the short, which is about stopping work at dark. Keep the people: 'Hold the child,
lose the grown-up.' Or use line 3, the mirror image, which ends well: 'Following, one finds what one seeks.' That gives 'Follow, and find
what you look for.'

history.text:
Warn clearly,
then bite.
history.why: FIRE over THUNDER: the kings made penalties clear and established the law, so clarity comes first and the bite second.
history.feedback: True: 'The ancient kings made penalties clear and established the law.' 'Warn clearly' is a fair plain version of making penalties clear beforehand. It matches the picture well: FIRE/lightning for clarity over THUNDER for the bite. It is short and a little funny, and it adds a condition to 'bite down': say it plainly first. Glad to post.

history.text:
When it thunders,
nothing pretends.
history.why: THUNDER moving under HEAVEN is the Image of all things without pretense, which is what Innocence means. (Kept as lines, not line 3: 26 and 27 are accepted line lessons, so a line here would be a third in a row.)
history.feedback:
True to the Image: 'Thunder moves beneath heaven, all things without pretense.' But it repeats the short. The meaning is already 'be straight / stop faking' and the question is 'Where are you performing?'. 'Nothing pretends' is the same point a third time. 'When it thunders, nothing pretends' also sounds mannered rather than like a person talking. The lines have better material: line 5, 'An illness without pretense. Do not medicate. There will be happiness.' That gives 'Not really sick?
Skip the medicine.' Or line 3, the tethered ox: 'The traveller's gain
is the town's loss.' To use a line here, change 26 or 27 to another kind. Otherwise use the other half of the Image: 'Kings fed everyone
by the seasons.'

history.text:
Small help, passed
through a window.
history.why: Line 4: a jug of wine and a basket of rice handed through the window, and in the end no fault; plain help counts in the pit.
history.feedback:
True to line 4: wine, rice, clay vessels 'handed through the window. In the end, no fault.' It adds to 'keep moving / small step': plain help is enough in the pit. The window matches the lit line. 'Small help' is a summary that throws away the concrete things that make the line memorable. Name them: 'Wine and rice,
through the window.' (16 and 18 chars). Or 'Just bread and wine
through a window.' is too long, so the first is better.

history.text:
This kind of pull
ends in marriage.
history.why: The Judgment says taking a wife resolves well: influence of this kind is not flirtation, it leads to marriage.
history.feedback:
Overclaims. The Judgment says 'Taking a wife resolves well'. It does not say influence 'ends in marriage'. 'This kind of pull' is vague: what kind? It also has nothing to do with the short, which is about listening while already having decided. A first-time viewer would take it as a fortune-cookie prediction. If it stays a judgment, keep it literal: 'A good time
to take a wife.' The line texts are more surprising and fit the lit line: the body sequence from toes (line 1) up to 'jaws, cheeks, and tongue' (line 6). Line 6 gives 'Moved, but only
in the mouth.' / 'All talk: jaw,
cheeks, tongue.' That also ends the 'already decided' short well.

history.text:
Great strength
watches its step.
history.why: THUNDER above HEAVEN is the most power in the highest place, and the Image says the realized person does not tread where it is not proper. (Not the ram line: 33 and 35 are accepted line lessons, so a line here would be a third in a row.)
history.feedback:
True to the Image: 'does not tread where it does not accord with propriety'. 'Watches its step' is a nice plain version of 'tread'. But it repeats the short almost word for word in meaning. The meaning is 'Mostly, know what not to do' and the question is 'What won't you do with it?'. The lesson adds nothing. The ram is the memorable material: line 3, 'The ram butts the hedge and entangles its horns'. That gives 'The ram butts the
hedge, gets stuck.' (check length) or 'Butt the hedge,
get your horns stuck.' It is worth changing 33 or 35 to another kind so 34 can have the ram. Otherwise use a judgment, but that one is thin ('Sustained orientation is supported').

history.text:
Blocked outside?
Work on yourself.
history.why: WATER on the MOUNTAIN cannot flow, and the Image says to turn inward and cultivate character. (Not line 1: 38 and 40 are accepted line lessons.)
history.feedback:
True: 'turns inward to cultivate character.' It is plain, but 'Work on yourself' is a generic self-help phrase, and it does not use the picture (WATER stuck on a MOUNTAIN). It also pulls against the short's own 'ask for help / Who could you ask?'. The best material is line 2, 'obstruction upon obstruction. It is not a personal matter.' That gives 'Blocked again?
It's not personal.' It is concrete, a little funny, and adds something. The repeated 'Going forward: obstruction. Coming back: praise' is also good: 'Can't go on?
Coming back helps.' Both are line lessons, so changing 38 or 40 to another kind would free this one. If it stays lines, tie it to the picture: 'Water can't climb
a mountain. Wait.' needs a check against the source. It is safer to keep the Image: 'Water stuck?
Look inward.'

history.text:
Even bad luck
can add to you.
history.why: Line 3: increased through unfortunate events, no fault, if you stay sincere and keep to the middle way.
history.feedback:
True to line 3: 'Increased through unfortunate events. No fault.' It is a real, slightly surprising takeaway, and it adds to 'go now / see good, move toward it'. Two things: 'bad luck' sits close to the fortune vocabulary the series avoids, and 'add to you' sounds a bit odd. 'Even bad events
can help you grow.' is too long for one line. Try 'Even bad times
can add to you.' or 'Bad things can
still increase you.'

history.text:
Go see someone
who can help.
history.why: The Judgment says to use this time to see the great person: rising goes faster with someone above to help. (Not line 3: 44 and 45 are accepted line lessons.)
history.feedback:
True: 'Use this time to see the great person. Do not worry.' It is plain and practical, it fits the Judgment page, and it adds to 'small steps / what can you add today'. 'Someone who can help' blurs 'the great person'; 'Go see someone
above you.' is closer to the text and more specific. Note that 39's meaning already says 'ask for help', so across the series this is the second 'get help' in a short span. It is not surprising enough to send to a friend.

history.text:
A red mountain,
keeping still.
history.why: Hokusai's Red Fuji is the Image of Keeping Still, mountain upon mountain, with nothing moving. (Not line 5: 53 and 54 are accepted line lessons.)

history.text:
With strength,
settle quarrels.
history.why: THUNDER and FIRE arrive together, force and clarity at once, and the Image says that is when to decide disputes. (Not line 6: 53-54 and 56-57 are accepted line lessons on both sides.)
history.feedback:
True to the Image: 'Thunder and lightning both arrive... decides disputes and carries out punishments.' But 'decide' overlaps the question 'What will you decide now?'. 'With strength' covers only the thunder and drops the fire/clarity half of the picture. 'Settle quarrels' is flat. This hexagram's most surprising material is the 'Big Dipper visible at midday' line (2/4): 'So many screens,
stars at noon.' It is strange and concrete, and it fits 'at your peak and worried'. It would need 56 or 54 changed. If it stays lines, use both trigrams: 'Thunder and light:
settle it now.'

history.text:
The good leave,
the petty move in.
history.why: Why things are stuck: the great departs, the small arrives, and the people who care are the ones pushed out.
history.feedback: The Judgment says 'Of inferior people... The great departs, the small arrives', and the synthesis says the configuration 'blocks the people who care'. Reading great and small as good and petty people is fair. It explains why things are stuck without repeating 'hold back' or 'turn down', and it suits the Judgment page. Line lengths are 15 and 18. Glad to post it.

history.text:
Follow, and find
what you look for.
history.why: Line 3 says plainly that following, one finds what one seeks.
history.feedback: The wording is in line 3 ('Following, one finds what one seeks'), but it is the flattest part of that line. It is abstract and sounds like a slogan. It has no link to the short's rest-at-nightfall theme and gives no picture. The concrete, surprising part of line 3 is the trade: 'Attached to the mature one. Losing the small child.' Try line 3 as 'Hold the grown one,\nlose the child.' (18/15), or line 2 reversed. Either says that following something means giving something else up, which the short does not say.

history.text:
Kings fed everyone
by the seasons.
history.why: The other half of the Image: the old kings fed all beings in step with the seasons, not forcing growth.
history.feedback: The Image does say this ('ancient kings nourished all beings in alignment with the seasons'), but viewers won't connect it to the thunder-under-heaven trigram picture, and 'kings fed everyone' teaches nothing about innocence or pretense. It is history trivia, not a takeaway. Line 5 is the surprising material and fits 'stop faking': 'An illness without pretense. Do not medicate. There will be happiness.' Try it as a line lesson: 'A real illness?\nDon't medicate.' Also possible is line 3's tethered ox (the traveler's gain is the townsperson's loss).

history.text:
Wine and rice
through a window.
history.why: Line 4: a jug of wine and a basket of rice handed through the window are enough, and in the end no fault.
history.feedback: True to line 4, and concrete and unusual, which is good. As written it is only an image with no point, close to the rejected 'Its shape: a watchtower.' A first-time viewer won't know what wine and rice through a window mean. The line's verdict is 'in the end, no fault': in a deep hole, a plain offering is enough. Add that point, e.g. 'Wine and rice\nare enough.' or 'A plain gift through\nthe window is enough' (shorten to fit 18). Keep line 4 as the source.

history.text:
A good time
to take a wife.
history.why: The Judgment's one concrete point: taking a wife resolves well.
history.feedback: The Judgment does say 'Taking a wife resolves well'. It is concrete, a little funny, and new to the short. But 'A good time to...' reads like a horoscope prediction, and it lets go of Influence's point about making room. It would reach 8 with a plainer quote that isn't a forecast, e.g. 'Taking a wife:\ngoes well.' Or use the body-part lines, which are the hexagram's most surprising material. Line 1: 'Influence in the big toes.' becomes 'It starts in\nthe big toes.' as a line lesson.

history.text:
Great power keeps
off wrong paths.
history.why: Thunder above heaven: the Image says the strong person does not tread where it is not right.
history.feedback: True to the Image, but it repeats the short: the meaning is 'Mostly, know what not to do' and the question is 'What won't you do with it?'. 'Keeps off wrong paths' is also stiff. Switch to line 3, which is vivid and funny: 'The ram butts the hedge and entangles its horns.' For example 'Ram butts hedge,\nhorns get stuck.' (16/16). The line also contrasts 'The petty person uses power. The realized person uses restraint', so the image carries the point on its own.

history.text:
Water can't flow?
Turn inward.
history.why: Water on the mountain cannot flow, and the Image says to turn inward and work on character.
history.feedback: 'Can't flow' comes from the synthesis and 'turns inward' from the Image, so it is true. But 'Turn inward' is vague and overlaps the short's 'The wall is the lesson'. The question-and-answer form also reads a bit cryptic. The line texts are better and repeat a pattern: 'Going forward: obstruction. Coming back: praise.' (line 1). A line lesson: 'Go on: blocked.\nCome back: praise.' (15/17). Or line 5 ('Great obstruction. Companions come.'), which pays off the short's 'ask for help': 'Badly stuck,\nfriends come.'

history.text:
Even bad events
can increase you.
history.why: Line 3: increased through unfortunate events, no fault.
history.feedback: True to line 3 ('Increased through unfortunate events. No fault.'). It is a real surprise and adds to a short about opportunity. 'Can increase you' is awkward English. A plainer version: 'Even bad events\ncan add to you.' or 'Bad things can\nincrease you too.' Fix the phrasing and it is an 8.

history.text:
Go see someone
above you.
history.why: The Judgment says to use this time to see the great person, without worry.
history.feedback: True to the Judgment ('Use this time to see the great person'). 'Someone above you' is a fair plain rendering. It is practical, fits a short about slow growth, avoids the 'don't worry' already used in the meaning, and suits the Judgment page. It is less surprising than the best lessons, but I would post it.

history.text:
Walk past people,
not seeing them.
history.why: The Judgment: walking through the courtyard, not seeing the people, no fault. Stillness inside while moving.
history.feedback:
True to the Judgment, and surprising. But on its own a viewer can take it as snubbing people, the opposite of the calm the hexagram teaches, and nothing says the stillness is inside you. Two options. Frame it: 'Walk through a crowd,
still inside.' (needs trimming to 18: 'Still inside,
even in a crowd.'). Or use line 5, 'Stilling the jaws. Words have order.', which answers the overthinking hook: 'Still your jaw;
words come in order' (shorten). The Red Fuji painting is also available here and would land at a glance, if the series needs a painting.

history.text:
See clearly,
act with force.
history.why: Thunder and lightning together: force and clarity at once, the pair the Image uses to judge cases.
history.feedback: Built from the synthesis (force and clarity), but abstract and generic. It sits close to the short's question 'What will you decide now?'. The Image's actual instruction is deciding disputes, and neither trigram picture makes 'see clearly, act with force' land. Abundance has striking line texts. Line 2/4: 'So abundant are the screens that the Big Dipper is visible at midday.' Line 6: 'So abundant his dwelling... desolate, no one there.' Try line 6: 'A huge house,\nno one inside.' (12/14). It is a real turn after 'Be the sun at noon'. Or line 2: 'So many screens,\nstars at noon.'
